```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 100)
```

When polygons overlap, their boundaries cross, and the question is usually not
"is this triangle inside?" but "which of the inputs cover this triangle?".
`depth` cannot answer that, because it counts boundaries crossed on the way in,
and boundaries from different inputs are mixed together. `edge_sources = TRUE`
keeps the link between every edge of the mesh and the input segments that made
it, and with that the coverage of every triangle can be found by walking the
mesh.

```{r setup}
library(cdtr)
```

## Four overlapping inputs

Feature 1 is a square with a square hole, 2 is a square that overlaps its
corner and part of the hole, 3 is a triangle across both, and 4 is a rectangle
that shares part of the left edge of feature 1. Outer rings run
counter-clockwise and holes run clockwise, so that an input's winding number
is 1 inside the feature and 0 outside, holes included.

```{r inputs}
rings <- list(
  list(feature = 1, xy = rbind(c(0, 0), c(4, 0), c(4, 4), c(0, 4))),
  list(feature = 1, xy = rbind(c(1, 1), c(1, 3), c(3, 3), c(3, 1))),
  list(feature = 2, xy = rbind(c(2.5, 2.5), c(5.5, 2.5), c(5.5, 5.5), c(2.5, 5.5))),
  list(feature = 3, xy = rbind(c(1, -0.5), c(3.5, 5), c(-0.5, 3))),
  list(feature = 4, xy = rbind(c(-0.8, 0.5), c(0, 0.5), c(0, 3.5), c(-0.8, 3.5))),
  ## a frame around everything, feature 0, which is not an input to be counted
  list(feature = 0, xy = rbind(c(-1, -1), c(7, -1), c(7, 7), c(-1, 7)))
)
```

The frame gives the mesh an outside that is covered by nothing. Without it the
mesh would only have the convex hull, which can be covered by an input.

Rings become vertices and segments, with an `owner` for each segment recording
its feature.

```{r pslg}
nv <- vapply(rings, function(r) nrow(r$xy), 1L)
first <- cumsum(c(0L, nv[-length(nv)]))
xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rings, `[[`, "xy"))
s0 <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(nv), function(k) first[k] + seq_len(nv[k])))
s1 <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(nv), function(k) first[k] + c(seq_len(nv[k])[-1], 1L)))
owner <- rep(vapply(rings, `[[`, 1, "feature"), nv)
length(s0)
```

## One triangulation for all of them

All the segments go in together. The crossings are found once, and become
vertices of the mesh.

```{r mesh}
r <- cdt_triangulate(xy[, 1], xy[, 2], s0, s1, edge_sources = TRUE)
table(r$origin)
c(fixed_edges = nrow(r$S), triangles = nrow(r$T))
```

There are more fixed edges than input segments, since a segment is split
wherever it crosses another, or where another vertex lies on it. The 14 vertices
with origin `"crossing"` are those splits.
`edge_sources` has one row for every fixed edge and every input segment
covering it.

```{r sources}
head(r$edge_sources)
table(n_inputs = table(r$edge_sources$edge))
```

`edge` is a row of `S`, `segment` is the position of the input segment in
`s0` and `s1`, and `forward` says whether the input runs the same way as the
`S` row. An edge covered by two input segments has two rows. That is where the
rectangle shares the left edge of the first square. The two segments run in
opposite directions, so one is `forward` and the other is not.

```{r shared}
multi <- as.integer(names(which(table(r$edge_sources$edge) > 1)))
r$edge_sources[r$edge_sources$edge %in% multi, ] |>
  transform(feature = owner[segment])
```

## Coverage by walking the mesh

Stepping from one triangle to its neighbour across an ordinary edge changes
nothing. Stepping across a fixed edge changes the winding number of each input
that covers it by plus or minus one, according to which way the input
runs. Starting from a triangle in the frame, where every winding number is 0,
the walk gives every triangle's winding number for each feature.

The function below does this, using only the mesh and `edge_sources`. It takes
the feature of each input segment, and a point known to be outside everything.

```{r walk}
mesh_winding <- function(r, owner, outside, n_features = max(owner)) {
  P <- r$P; T <- r$T; S <- r$S; es <- r$edge_sources
  nt <- nrow(T)
  key <- function(a, b) paste(pmin(a, b), pmax(a, b))

  ## winding change for each feature on crossing an S row from right to left
  delta <- matrix(0L, nrow(S), n_features)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(es))) {
    f <- owner[es$segment[i]]
    if (f > 0) delta[es$edge[i], f] <- delta[es$edge[i], f] + if (es$forward[i]) 1L else -1L
  }

  ## every triangle edge, with its triangle and the opposite vertex
  e <- rbind(cbind(T[, 1], T[, 2], seq_len(nt), T[, 3]),
             cbind(T[, 2], T[, 3], seq_len(nt), T[, 1]),
             cbind(T[, 3], T[, 1], seq_len(nt), T[, 2]))
  k <- key(e[, 1], e[, 2])
  s_row <- match(k, key(S[, 1], S[, 2]))
  pairs <- split(seq_len(nrow(e)), k)
  nb <- vector("list", nt)
  for (p in pairs[lengths(pairs) == 2L]) {
    nb[[e[p[1], 3]]] <- c(nb[[e[p[1], 3]]], p[2])
    nb[[e[p[2], 3]]] <- c(nb[[e[p[2], 3]]], p[1])
  }

  w <- matrix(NA_integer_, nt, n_features)
  start <- cdt_locate(P, T, outside[1], outside[2])
  w[start, ] <- 0L
  queue <- start
  while (length(queue)) {
    t <- queue[1]; queue <- queue[-1]
    for (j in nb[[t]]) {
      u <- e[j, 3]
      if (!anyNA(w[u, ])) next
      sr <- s_row[j]
      if (is.na(sr)) {
        w[u, ] <- w[t, ]
      } else {
        a <- S[sr, 1]; b <- S[sr, 2]; c <- e[j, 4]
        left <- (P[b, 1] - P[a, 1]) * (P[c, 2] - P[a, 2]) -
          (P[b, 2] - P[a, 2]) * (P[c, 1] - P[a, 1])
        w[u, ] <- w[t, ] + sign(left) * delta[sr, ]
      }
      queue <- c(queue, u)
    }
  }
  w
}

w <- mesh_winding(r, owner, outside = c(-0.9, -0.9))
anyNA(w)
head(w)
```

Row `i` of `w` is triangle `i` of `r$T`, and column `j` is feature `j`. The walk
reaches every triangle, since the mesh is connected.

## Checking it

Coverage is the winding number being non-zero. An independent check is a
point-in-polygon test of each triangle's centre, ring by ring.

```{r check}
centre <- function(r) {
  cbind(rowMeans(matrix(r$P[t(r$T), 1], ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)),
        rowMeans(matrix(r$P[t(r$T), 2], ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)))
}
inside_ring <- function(p, ring) {
  j <- nrow(ring); inside <- rep(FALSE, nrow(p))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(ring))) {
    cross <- ((ring[i, 2] > p[, 2]) != (ring[j, 2] > p[, 2])) &
      (p[, 1] < (ring[j, 1] - ring[i, 1]) * (p[, 2] - ring[i, 2]) /
         (ring[j, 2] - ring[i, 2]) + ring[i, 1])
    inside <- xor(inside, cross); j <- i
  }
  inside
}
p <- centre(r)
truth <- sapply(1:4, function(f) {
  inside <- rep(FALSE, nrow(p))
  for (ring in rings) if (ring$feature == f) inside <- xor(inside, inside_ring(p, ring$xy))
  inside
})
all((w != 0) == truth)
```

The two agree for every triangle. The test above needs a coordinate for every
triangle and every ring, where the walk only needs the segments.

## What depth cannot say

`depth` is still useful, but it is the number of boundaries between a triangle and
the outside, not the number of features covering it. Here it is compared with
the number of features that do cover each triangle.

```{r depth}
table(depth = r$depth, covered_by = rowSums(w != 0))
```

Depth 3 mixes triangles covered by no feature with triangles covered by two.
A triangle in the hole of feature 1, away from the other features, is three
boundaries in from the frame (the frame, the outer ring of 1 and its hole) and
is covered by nothing. A triangle in feature 1 that also lies in feature 2 is
also three boundaries in, and is covered twice. No function of `depth` can tell
these apart, while the walk can.

## Pieces by the set of covering features

Triangles with the same set of covering features make an overlay piece. This
is what an overlay or intersection of the inputs is made of.

```{r pieces}
set <- apply(w != 0, 1, function(i) paste(which(i), collapse = "+"))
set[set == ""] <- "none"
area <- function(r) {
  a <- r$P[r$T[, 1], ]; b <- r$P[r$T[, 2], ]; c <- r$P[r$T[, 3], ]
  0.5 * abs((b[, 1] - a[, 1]) * (c[, 2] - a[, 2]) - (c[, 1] - a[, 1]) * (b[, 2] - a[, 2]))
}
sort(round(tapply(area(r), set, sum), 3), decreasing = TRUE)
```

```{r plot}
sets <- sort(unique(set))
pal <- hcl.colors(length(sets), "Set 3", alpha = 0.8)
pal[sets == "none"] <- "grey92"
col <- pal[match(set, sets)]
tri <- t(cbind(r$T, NA))
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(r$P, type = "n", asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
polygon(r$P[tri, 1], r$P[tri, 2], col = col, border = "grey80", lwd = 0.5)
segments(r$P[r$S[, 1], 1], r$P[r$S[, 1], 2], r$P[r$S[, 2], 1], r$P[r$S[, 2], 2], lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", legend = sets, fill = pal,
       cex = 0.7, bty = "n", title = "covered by")
par(op)
```

## Notes

The walk here does not depend on the mesh being refined, so it works with
`max_area` and `min_angle` too, since `edge_sources` follows each input through
splits by refinement. The polymer package does this at scale for polygon layers
from any source, and uses wkpool for the shared vertices.
